standard: ASD-STE100 adaptation for software engineering, DevOps, SRE, and IT
note: Doc-verified controlled terminology. Per domain: approved technical nouns and verbs (not flagged by the linter), alias->canonical mappings (one name for one thing), and terms to avoid with preferred replacements. Consumed by scripts/ste-lint.py. See each domain's 'sources' for provenance.

availability zone.note: A physically separate location within an Azure region.

resource group.note: Container that holds related resources for an Azure solution.

Azure Resource Manager.note: The deployment and management service and control plane for Azure.

virtual machine scale set.note: A group of identical, load-balanced VMs that can autoscale.

virtual network.note: Isolated network in Azure. Docs spell it VNet.

network security group.note: Filters inbound and outbound traffic to Azure resources.

Azure role-based access control.note: Authorization system built on Azure Resource Manager.

Microsoft Entra ID.note: Cloud identity service. Renamed from Azure Active Directory.

master/slave.reason: Non-inclusive. Microsoft style replaces this pair with primary and subordinate.

demilitarized zone (DMZ).reason: Militaristic term. Microsoft style uses perimeter network.

hang.reason: Microsoft style avoids hang for a stalled app or service.

Azure Active Directory.reason: Deprecated product name. Azure Active Directory was renamed to Microsoft Entra ID.

Cloud Storage.note: Object storage service. Canonical name is Cloud Storage, not GCS.

BigQuery.note: Serverless data warehouse. One word, camel case.

Identity and Access Management.note: Access control service for Google Cloud resources.

managed instance group.note: A group of identical VM instances managed as a unit.

Pub/Sub.note: Asynchronous messaging service. Canonical spelling is Pub/Sub.

whitelist.reason: Non-inclusive. Google style recommends allowlist, trustlist, or safelist.

blacklist.reason: Non-inclusive. Google style recommends denylist, blocklist, or excludelist.

master/slave.reason: Non-inclusive. Google style uses primary or main for master, and replica or worker for slave.

native.reason: Ambiguous. Google style prefers built-in or a more specific term when referring to software.

Availability Zone.note: A distinct, isolated location within an AWS Region.

Amazon Simple Storage Service.note: Object storage service. Commonly referred to as S3.

S3 bucket.note: A container for objects stored in Amazon S3.

Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud.note: Resizable compute capacity as virtual server instances.

Amazon Virtual Private Cloud.note: Logically isolated virtual network in AWS.

AWS Identity and Access Management.note: Access control service for AWS resources.

Amazon Elastic Block Store.note: Block storage volumes for EC2 instances.

Amazon Machine Image.note: Template that defines an EC2 instance at launch.

AWS Key Management Service.note: Managed key creation and control service.

network ACL.note: Stateless traffic filter at the subnet boundary.

whitelist.reason: Non-inclusive. AWS documentation uses allow list, for example in Network Firewall and Macie.

blacklist.reason: Non-inclusive. AWS documentation uses deny list, for example in IAM policy evaluation and Organizations SCPs.

master.reason: In database replication contexts AWS RDS uses primary DB instance and read replica, not master.

slave.reason: In database replication contexts AWS RDS uses read replica, not slave.

Datadog.note: Short forms for the product name Datadog.

APM.note: APM is Datadog's tracing and service performance product.

RUM.note: RUM captures front-end browser and mobile sessions.

SLO.note: SLO is a target for service reliability.

SLI.note: SLI is the measured signal behind an SLO.

Datadog Agent.note: The collector process that reports data to Datadog.

Cloud Security Management.note: CSM is Datadog's cloud security posture and workload product.

Synthetic Monitoring.note: Scripted API and browser tests run from Datadog.

Kubernetes.note: k8s is the numeronym (k + 8 letters + s); kube is the common short form.

control plane.note: master is the historical term; docs now use control plane.

HorizontalPodAutoscaler.note: HPA scales workload replicas on observed load.

PersistentVolumeClaim.note: A user request for storage bound to a PersistentVolume.

CustomResourceDefinition.note: Defines a custom resource type in the API.

ServiceAccount.note: Identity for processes running in Pods.

master node.reason: Kubernetes docs name the components that manage the cluster the control plane; master is non-inclusive and no longer used.

master.reason: Same inclusive-naming change; the cluster management layer is the control plane.

dockershim.reason: dockershim was removed in Kubernetes v1.24; the kubelet requires a runtime that conforms to the Container Runtime Interface.

Docker Compose.note: Current CLI is invoked as docker compose (Compose V2); docker-compose is the legacy V1 binary.

Docker Engine.note: dockerd is the daemon process of Docker Engine.

BuildKit.note: The default build backend for Docker builds.

image.note: A read-only template used to create containers.

registry.note: A service that stores and distributes images.

MAINTAINER.reason: The MAINTAINER Dockerfile instruction is deprecated; LABEL is the flexible replacement for image metadata.

docker-compose.reason: Compose V1 (the Python docker-compose binary) reached end of life; Compose V2 is invoked as docker compose.

container links.reason: Legacy container links (--link) are a deprecated Engine feature; connect containers with user-defined networks instead.

repository.note: "repo" is common shorthand; the glossary term is "repository".

working tree.note: Glossary uses "working tree". "worktree" is the distinct linked-worktree feature (git worktree).

index.note: Glossary term is "index". "staging area" and "cache" are informal synonyms for the same store.

remote-tracking branch.note: A ref that follows a branch on a remote, e.g. origin/main.

object name.note: Glossary term is "object name" (a 40-hex or abbreviated hash).

pull request.note: Not a core Git concept. "PR" (GitHub) and "MR" (GitLab) are platform features; the Git-native analog is git request-pull plus fetch/merge.

master.reason: "master" is the historic Git default branch name and is still the current fallback, but git-init documents that the default will change to "main" in Git 3.0 and is already overridable via init.defaultBranch. "main" is the widely preferred name and the default on GitHub and GitLab.

whitelist.reason: Non-inclusive and non-self-describing. Inclusive Naming Initiative tier-1 replacement; adopted across the Git project.

blacklist.reason: Non-inclusive and non-self-describing. The Git project moved to "allowlist"/"denylist" tree-wide because the terms are self-defining.

work item.note: Jira Cloud renamed "issue" to "work item" in the UI (the REST API still uses "issue"). "ticket" is JSM/informal; "card" is the board representation of a work item.

backlog refinement.note: Atlassian agile guidance uses "backlog refinement" for the ongoing activity of reviewing and re-ordering the backlog.

story point.note: Unit of relative estimation; "story point" is the canonical Atlassian term.

subtask.note: A child work item of a standard work item.

JQL.note: Structured search language for Jira; keep the acronym uppercase.

grooming.reason: "grooming" (backlog grooming) has fallen out of favor in the agile community due to negative connotations; Atlassian documents the activity as "backlog refinement".

whitelist.reason: Non-inclusive; Atlassian administration docs use "allowlist" for IP and domain allow rules.

blacklist.reason: Non-inclusive and non-self-describing; use "denylist" (or "blocklist") for blocked entries.

Opsgenie.note: Atlassian writes the product name as "Opsgenie" (one word, single capital O).

on-call schedule.note: A schedule contains one or more rotations that define who is on call and when.

escalation policy.note: When an alert's responders field is set to an escalation policy, Opsgenie uses it to decide who to notify, when, and in what order.

responder.note: Newer Opsgenie UI/API v2 uses "responder" (user, team, or escalation notified about an alert). "recipient" is the older term.

alias.note: Client-defined identifier used to de-duplicate alerts; alerts with the same alias are merged.

recipient.reason: Opsgenie standardized on "responder" for the users, teams, and escalations notified about an alert; "recipient" is the legacy v1 term.

whitelist.reason: Non-inclusive and non-self-describing; use "allowlist" for allowed IPs and integration sources.

blacklist.reason: Non-inclusive and non-self-describing; use "denylist" (or "blocklist") for blocked entries.

nullable reference type.note: A reference type T? in a nullable-aware context. Same .NET type as T; the compiler tracks null-state. Distinct from a nullable value type.

nullable value type.note: An instance of System.Nullable<T> that adds a null value to a value type. Distinct from a nullable reference type.

LINQ query.note: Language-Integrated Query. Write in query syntax (from/where/select) or method syntax; both compile to the same operators.

delegate.note: A reference type that references a method. Basis for events and lambda expressions.

Linq.reason: acronym for Language-Integrated Query, always written in uppercase in the docs

nullable type.prefer: nullable reference type or nullable value type
nullable type.reason: the two are different .NET constructs; the docs document them on separate pages and the ambiguous term hides which one is meant

C-Sharp.reason: the language name is C# in official documentation

discriminated union.note: A type whose value is one of several named cases, each optionally carrying data. Has structural equality.

computation expression.note: A convenient syntax for computations that can be sequenced and combined, such as async, seq, and query.

pipeline operator.note: The |> operator passes a value as the last argument to a function, so calls read left to right.

immutable value.note: F# values are immutable by default; use the mutable keyword to opt in to in-place change.

units of measure.note: Compile-time annotations on numeric types for dimensions such as length or mass. Checked at compile time, erased at run time.

F-Sharp.reason: the language name is F# in official documentation

enum (for a discriminated union).reason: an F# enumeration and a discriminated union are different constructs; a DU carries data per case while an enum maps names to constant values

variable (for a let binding).reason: F# let bindings are immutable values by default, not variables; the docs reserve variable for mutable state

.NET.note: The current unified, cross-platform implementation (5.0 and later). It succeeds .NET Core; the version was named 5 rather than 4 to avoid confusion with .NET Framework 4.x. Distinct from .NET Framework.

.NET Framework.note: The original Windows-only implementation (versions 1.x through 4.x). Still shipped with Windows, but new development should use modern .NET. Distinct from .NET (5+); the two are different products, not versions of one line.

common language runtime.note: The execution engine for managed code: memory management, JIT compilation, type safety. The .NET (Core) CLR is cross-platform; the .NET Framework CLR is Windows only.

garbage collector.note: The CLR subsystem that reclaims memory for managed objects no longer in use.

base class library.note: The System.* (and limited Microsoft.*) libraries that higher-level frameworks build on.

common intermediate language.note: The CPU-independent instruction set that compilers emit; the JIT compiler converts it to native code at run time.

target framework moniker.note: The canonical framework identity (for example .NETCoreApp,Version=v10.0). The TargetFramework project value (net10.0) is a friendly alias the SDK translates into the TFM.

just-in-time compiler.note: Translates CIL to native machine code at execution time.

.NET Core.reason: the Core suffix was dropped at .NET 5 to mark it as the main implementation going forward; the last release named .NET Core was 3.1

.NET Core 4.reason: version numbers 4.x were skipped to avoid confusion with .NET Framework 4.x; .NET Core 3.1 was followed by .NET 5

netcoreapp.reason: the short target-framework moniker changed from netcoreapp (for example netcoreapp3.1) to net (for example net5.0) starting in .NET 5

.Net.reason: the platform name is .NET, written with an uppercase NET, throughout the documentation

Nuget.reason: the package manager name is NuGet with an uppercase G in official documentation

Go.note: The language name is just Go. The 'golang' moniker came only from the original web domain golang.org and is a handy label/tag (#golang), not the formal name (go.dev/doc/faq). The plural 'goroutines' is fine.

goroutine.note: One word, lowercase: goroutine. Named to avoid the inaccurate connotations of thread/coroutine/process (go.dev/doc/effective_go).

defer statement.note: The construct is the 'defer statement'; the scheduled call is the 'deferred function'. Use 'defer' as the verb (go.dev/doc/effective_go).

Golang.reason: Not the formal language name. The FAQ states the name is 'just plain Go, regardless'; golang is only the old web domain and social tag. Use Go in prose; 'golang' is acceptable only in package paths, tags, or URLs.

GO.reason: All-caps GO is wrong. Although the logo uses two capital letters, the language name is written Go.

go routine.reason: Spelled as one word, lowercase. 'go routine', 'go-routine', and 'green thread' are non-canonical.

JavaScript.note: Canonical casing is JavaScript (capital J, capital S). 'JS' is an accepted short form but spell out JavaScript on first use in formal prose. 'Javascript'/'javascript' are misspellings of the name.

ECMAScript.note: ECMAScript is the standard/specification name (TC39, tc39.es). It is NOT a synonym for JavaScript in prose: JavaScript is the language, ECMAScript is the spec it implements. Version tags like ES2015 refer to spec editions.

arrow function.note: Canonical term is 'arrow function'. 'fat arrow' and 'lambda' are informal and non-canonical on MDN.

immediately invoked function expression.note: Canonical is 'immediately invoked function expression (IIFE)'. 'self-invoking'/'self-executing function' are non-canonical.

var.reason: MDN style guide and the let reference recommend const over let whenever a variable is not reassigned, and let over var. var is function-scoped and hoisted (initialized as undefined), which causes scoping and hoisting surprises that block-scoped const/let avoid.

Javascript.reason: Wrong casing. The proper name is JavaScript with a capital J and capital S.

fat arrow.reason: Informal slang. MDN's canonical term is 'arrow function'.

self-executing function.reason: Non-canonical. MDN uses 'immediately invoked function expression (IIFE)'.

object-oriented programming.note: Spell out on first use, then OOP is acceptable. Use 'object-oriented' (hyphenated) as the adjective.

constructor.note: Prefer 'constructor' in prose. 'ctor' is code shorthand only.

finalizer.note: .NET docs use 'finalizer'; 'destructor' is the C++/C# keyword-level term. Pick one per document.

dependency injection.note: Spell out first, then DI. It is a technique for achieving inversion of control.

base class.note: .NET docs canonical term is 'base class'. Use one label consistently.

override.replacement: override (runtime replacement of a base member) vs overload (same name, different signature)
override.reason: Writers conflate the two. 'Override' means a derived class replaces a virtual base member; 'overload' means multiple methods share a name but differ in parameters. They are unrelated mechanisms.

inheritance (when composition is meant).reason: Reusing behavior by holding another object as a member is composition, not inheritance. Do not call a 'has-a' relationship inheritance; inheritance is an 'is-a' relationship.

object (when class is meant).reason: A class is the blueprint (a type definition); an object is a runtime instance allocated from that blueprint. Do not use them interchangeably.

interface (when abstract class is meant).reason: An interface declares members with no state or implementation contract role; an abstract class can carry state and partial implementation. Name the exact construct.

higher-order function.note: A function that takes a function as an argument or returns a function. Spell out first, then HOF.

algebraic data type.note: Spell out first. Beware collision: ADT can also mean 'abstract data type' in OOP, so avoid the acronym in mixed-domain docs.

functional programming.note: Spell out on first use, then FP.

discriminated union.note: F# canonical term is 'discriminated union'. 'Sum type' is the type-theory term for the same idea.

referential transparency.note: An expression is referentially transparent if it can be replaced by its value without changing program behavior.

first-class function.note: Functions treated like any other value: assigned, passed, and returned. F# docs use 'function value'.

lambda expression.note: An unnamed function. Use 'lambda expression' in formal prose.

functor (as a synonym for function).replacement: functor = a type that can be mapped over (defines map); function = a mapping from inputs to outputs
functor (as a synonym for function).reason: A functor is not a function. In FP a functor is a container/type that implements a lawful 'map' operation. Calling any function object a 'functor' (a C++-ism) confuses readers in an FP context.

monad (as 'a wrapper' or vague hand-wave.replacement: monad = a type with 'return'/unit and 'bind' (flatMap) that obey the monad laws
monad (as 'a wrapper' or vague hand-wave.reason: 'Monad' has a precise definition: a type constructor plus unit and bind operations satisfying left identity, right identity, and associativity. Do not use it loosely to mean any box or wrapper.

currying (used to mean partial applicati.replacement: currying = converting an n-argument function into nested single-argument functions; partial application = fixing some arguments to get a function of the remaining ones
currying (used to mean partial applicati.reason: The two are related but distinct. Currying changes a function's shape; partial application supplies some arguments. Name the one you mean.

pure function (applied to a function wit.replacement: pure function (no side effects, output depends only on inputs) vs impure function
pure function (applied to a function wit.reason: A function that performs I/O, mutates shared state, or reads a clock is not pure. Reserve 'pure' for functions that are referentially transparent.
